newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Pensions report boosts UK EU money opponents.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Pensions report boosts UK EU money opponents.

text.p: Opponents of British membership of a single European currency were given a major boost on Thursday when a parliamentary committee warned it could mean either higher interest rates or mounting inflation.

The Social Security Committee said in a report that if Britain abandoned the pound sterling, it could find itself paying the penalty for massive state pension liabilities in Germany, France, Italy and other European Union countries.

"Taxpayers in the United Kingdom, whose pensions derive largely from funded occupational pension schemes, could find themselves subsidising the large unfunded pension liabilities of other member states," the report of the all-party group said.

But the European Commission denied the Committee's claims. "It is inconceivable that the UK would be required to pay the future pension costs of people in other member states," Geoffrey Martin, head of its British representation, said in a statement.
The statement also said any EU country borrowing heavily to fund its pension liabilities could, under the rules of Stage Three of Economic and Monetary Union, face heavy fines.
In Britain, most firms have occupational pension schemes generally funded by company and employee contributions.

The committee report noted that a recent Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) report estimated public pension schemes in Britain would cost nearly 19 percent of annual gross domestic product to fund now.
By contrast, the figures for France, Italy and Germany were about 98, 113 and 139 percent, respectively.
The committee also said British national debt plus unfunded pension liabilities averaged 9,000 pounds ($14,650) per head.
"If we also took on our share of the unfunded pension liabilities of the EU, that figure would increase to some 30,000 pounds ($48,850) for every man, woman and child," it said.

So-called Eurosceptic members of the committee were quick to latch on to the report. "From a personal perspective, I believe if we join the single currency, we will be giving away our competitive position," said Conservative David Shaw.

Other committee members said the issue should be key to Britain's decision on whether to adopt the Euro currency, due to be launched in 1999. Both the ruling Conservative and opposition Labour parties are taking a wait-and-see attitude.
The report also noted popular unrest in France and Germany after attempts to curtail social provision.

"It is likely, therefore, that alternative ways of meeting current costs will be employed. One risk would be that the European Central Bank would come under pressure to relax monetary policy by printing money," it said.
"Another risk is that countries might seek to borrow their way out of financial pressures caused by rising social security bills," the report added.

If this happened, "bond issuance from hard-pressed European Union governments would raise (other things being equal) yields on Euro-denominated bonds". This would increase British interest rates and industrial costs and damage employment prospects.

The committee said Britain should press EU finance ministers to commission experts to produce figures on unfunded pension liabilities in member states. These should then be taken into account "in the decision to be made in 1998 on which countries will be eligible for Economic and Monetary Union," it said.

Pensions minister Oliver Heald welcomed the recognition that British pensions were much better funded than those in most of Europe. "We will be considering the report in detail," he said. ($1=.6141 Pound)
